The ashes from the first great war still darken the snow. The capitalistic city-state known simply as “The Factory”, which fueled the war with heavily armored mechs, has closed its doors, drawing the attention of several nearby countries. Scythe is an engine-building game set in an alternate-history 1920s period. It is a time of farming and war, broken hearts and rusted gears, innovation and valor. In Scythe, each player represents a character from one of five factions of Eastern Europe who are attempting to earn their fortune and claim their faction's stake in the land around the mysterious Factory. Players conquer territory, enlist new recruits, reap resources, gain villagers, build structures, and activate monstrous mechs. Scythe gives players almost complete control over their fate. Other than each player’s individual hidden objective card, the only elements of luck or variability are “encounter” cards that players will draw as they interact with the citizens of newly explored lands. Each encounter card provides the player with several options, allowing them to mitigate the luck of the draw through their selection. Combat is also driven by choices, not luck or randomness. Objectives Each player starts with two objectives, you can only complete one of these. When you do, gain a star for completing the objective and discard the one you didn't. Turn On your turn, move your action piece to one of the action spaces on your player mat other than the space you were on last turn. (You may not take the same action two turns in a row) 1. On the new space, first resolve the upper action, if desired. (The Upper actions and how to take them are described below) 2. Then, resolve the lower action, if desired. (The Lower actions and how to take them are described below) You may perform no actions if you wish, but still must move to another action space on the start of your next turn. • After to taking up to 2 actions, you may then resolve objectives if they apply • Each player is a Faction, and this brings with it unique bonuses and abilities Actions Each player board has slightly different pairings of top and lower actions, but everyone can perform the same actions in some combination. • The Cost of the lower actions vary per player, but all have something that costs 2/3/4/4 • Upper action benefits start with cubes on them which stops you from gaining the full benefit. • Lower action costs have some of the cost in a broken black border which forms part of the cost at start of game. • There are ways of moving cubes from blocking benefits to blocking costs as long as they have that broken black border Note: The squares with a red background are costs . The squares with a green background is a benefit you gain from taking the action. [Rating: 1/10] The artwork of this game is plagiarized.  Jakub Rozalski is a sham.  More info here: https://www.reddit.com/r/conceptart/comments/853k2g/the_truth_behind_the_art_of_jakub_rozalski/

[Rating: 1/10] I don't like that the "bottom-row actions" on the player boards become useless in the later part of the game. For example when you have built all your buildings, the build action is then pointless. Unfortunately this is true for ALL the bottom-row actions. Why can you do less after you developed your faction? This aspect of gameplay is highly unsatisfying for me. I will have to play the game a couple more times to see if this really bothers me.  Yes, you can keep using the bottom-row actions just for the money / bonuses, but they cost the same as if using them fully, which makes no sense: "So 

[Rating: 1/10] The world of the game plagiarized Dust tactics! Cavalry was ridiculous in front of tanks in the 20s, in front of walkers it is even more of a laughing stock. If all these walkers come from one source ('Factory') why they different for different nations? Gameplay is not innovative as well. Artworks are the best part of this project, but even they lack details so badly.

[Rating: 1/10] I can't help but think this game is just so beautiful. I wanted to love it. I tried so hard to love it. Everything is full of bling, it should be right up my alley. Euro and conflict in one, on paper this game was exactly the right game for me. In reality though I found the combat tedious and boring, I found the euro aspect tedious and boring, and all I was left with was a beautiful game to look at and never want to play. Not a bad game. But not a good game either. I have actually written a full review on it.

[Rating: 1/10] I have played this game twice now and both times I had a terrible experience playing. But to do, you need to blow all of your might (which in turn is actually vp) to win a battle. After winning the battle, you notice that you have become an easy target, all because you needed to stop your goods from getting lost.   Or you could use your goods. The more and more I wanted to like the game, the more and more everything about it turned me off: theme, mechanics, miniatures, production, etc. During the KS project I printed out a print and play copy to play & test. Got pieces together and read the rules.  It all fell flat. It's hyped as a 4X game. It's barely 2X and those two parts are half way done.
